headline: UK publishes the legal texts of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's reset deals with the EU

terms.meaning: A scheme where firms must pay for the carbon they release, with permits that can be bought and sold.
An agreement letting young people live and work in another country for a limited time.

levels.headline: UK publishes the legal texts of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's reset deals with the EU
levels.body:
The government has published the legal texts of the agreements that Prime Minister Andy Burnham reached with the European Union at a summit in Brussels on 20 November. The documents cover food and farming standards, the linking of the UK and EU emissions trading systems, and a youth mobility scheme.
Burnham has described the package as a "win-win" for both sides. Publication allows MPs, businesses and campaigners to examine the detail of what has been agreed, rather than relying on summaries.
The deal remains politically contentious. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage accused Burnham of betraying Brexit as the summit got under way, and has demanded a referendum if Labour ever seeks to rejoin the EU. Burnham has said a vote on rejoining could feature in a future election manifesto, but that holding one now would not be right.
levels.why: The texts show how far the UK is prepared to align with EU rules, a question that will shape the next election.

levels.headline: The government shows the detailed legal wording of its new deals with Europe
levels.body:
The government has now published the full legal wording of the deals Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed with the European Union in Brussels on 20 November. The texts deal with food and farming standards, a link between UK and EU carbon trading schemes, and a scheme for young people to live and work abroad.
Mr Burnham calls the package a "win-win". Releasing the detail means MPs, firms and campaigners can see exactly what has been promised.
The deal is still disputed. Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, says it betrays Brexit and wants a referendum if Labour tries to rejoin the EU. Mr Burnham says a vote on rejoining could appear in a future manifesto, though he does not think now is the right time.
levels.why: People can now judge the deal on its detail, and it will feed the argument over Britain's place in Europe.

levels.headline: Full texts of the UK's new agreements with the EU are made public
levels.body:
The UK government has put out the complete legal texts of the agreements Prime Minister Andy Burnham made with the European Union in Brussels on 20 November. They cover food and farming rules, a link between the two sides' schemes for pricing carbon, and a youth mobility scheme that lets young people work and live in each other's countries for a set time.
Mr Burnham says the deal is good for both sides. Publishing the wording lets people check what has really been agreed.
Critics disagree strongly. Reform UK's Nigel Farage says it betrays Brexit and calls for a referendum if Labour wants to rejoin. Mr Burnham says a vote on rejoining could be in a future manifesto but is not right for now.
levels.why: The wording will decide how much UK rules follow EU rules, which affects trade, food and young people's opportunities.

levels.headline: The government publishes the full wording of its deals with the EU
levels.body:
The government has published the full legal wording of the deals that Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed with the European Union. He struck them at a summit in Brussels on 20 November. They cover food and farming rules, a link between the UK and EU carbon trading schemes, and a scheme that would let young people live and work abroad.
Mr Burnham calls the deal a "win-win", meaning both sides gain. Anyone can now read what was agreed.
Nigel Farage, who leads Reform UK, says the deal is a betrayal of Brexit. He wants a vote if Labour ever tries to rejoin the EU. Mr Burnham says a vote could be in a future manifesto, but that it is not the right time now.
levels.why: It shows what the UK has promised the EU, and it keeps the debate about Brexit alive.

levels.headline: Britain shares the exact wording of its new agreements with the EU
levels.body:
The UK government has now shared the exact wording of the agreements it made with the European Union. Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed them in Brussels on 20 November. They are about food and farming standards, a link between the carbon markets of the UK and the EU (where companies pay for the pollution they cause), and a plan for young people to live and work in each other's countries.
Mr Burnham says the deal is a "win-win" and helps both sides.
Some people are angry. Nigel Farage says it betrays Brexit and wants a referendum if Labour tries to rejoin. Mr Burnham says that could be in a future manifesto, the plan a party shares before an election, but not now.
levels.why: It lets everyone see what the UK has agreed, and the arguments about Europe are far from over.

levels.headline: The UK has published the details of its new deals with Europe
levels.body:
The UK government has published the details of its new deals with the European Union. Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed them in Brussels on 20 November. The deals cover food and farming rules, a link between how the two sides charge companies for carbon pollution, and a plan for young people to live and work in each other's countries for a while.
Mr Burnham says the deals are good for both sides. Putting the words in public means people can check them.
Not everyone is happy. Nigel Farage says the deals go against Brexit, when the UK left the EU. He wants a public vote if Labour tries to rejoin. Mr Burnham says that idea could come up in a future election plan, but not yet.
levels.why: People can now read what has been agreed, and the debate about the UK and Europe goes on.

levels.headline: The UK has shared the small print of its new deals with Europe
levels.body:
The government has shared the small print of its new deals with the European Union. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, agreed them in Brussels on 20 November. The deals are about food and farming rules, about charging companies for the pollution they cause, and about letting young people live and work in each other's countries.
Mr Burnham says both sides win. Now that the words are public, MPs, who are chosen by voters to make laws, can read them closely.
Nigel Farage, who led the push for Brexit, says the deals betray it. He wants a referendum, which is a vote by everyone, if Labour tries to rejoin the EU. Mr Burnham says a vote might be in a future plan for an election, but not now.
levels.why: It matters because the deals could change trade, food rules and chances for young people.

levels.headline: The government has put the full details of its Europe deals online
levels.body:
The government has put the full details of its new deals with Europe online. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, agreed the deals on 20 November in Brussels, the capital of Belgium, where the European Union meets. They are about food and farming, about making companies pay for pollution, and about young people being able to work and live abroad.
Mr Burnham says it is a "win-win". That means both sides get something good.
Nigel Farage does not agree. He says the deals go against Brexit, which was when the UK left the EU. He wants a vote of the public if Labour tries to rejoin. Mr Burnham says that might be in a plan for a future election, but it is not right for now.
levels.why: Now people can read the deals for themselves and decide what they think.

levels.headline: Britain has shown everyone the written deals it made with Europe
levels.body:
Britain has shown everyone the written deals it made with Europe. The leader of the country, Andy Burnham, made the deals in a big meeting in Brussels. Brussels is a city where European leaders meet. The deals are about food and farms, about making firms pay for pollution, and about young people being allowed to work in other countries.
Mr Burnham says both sides win. Now anybody can read the papers and see what was agreed.
Some people are cross. Nigel Farage says the deals go against Brexit. Brexit was when Britain left the group of European countries. He wants everyone to vote if Labour tries to join again. Mr Burnham says maybe later, but not now.
levels.why: Everyone can see what was promised, and people still disagree about it.

levels.headline: Britain has written down a new deal with its neighbours in Europe
levels.body:
Imagine your class made a deal with the class next door. They agreed to share some rules about food and farms, to make sure everyone cleans up after themselves, and to let some children visit and play in each other's rooms. Now the teacher has written the deal down for all to see.
That is a bit like what has happened. Britain's leader, Andy Burnham, made a deal with the countries of Europe, and the written deal is now public.
Some people like it. Mr Burnham says it is good for both sides. Others, like Nigel Farage, do not. He thinks Britain should have stayed apart. People will keep talking about who is right.
levels.why: It shows how Britain wants to get along with its neighbours.

headline: S&P 500 closes up 1.6% at 7,297.49 as tech leads rebound in shortened Black Friday session

terms.meaning: A stock index dominated by technology companies.
A fall of at least 10% from a recent peak.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes up 1.6% at 7,297.49 as tech leads rebound in shortened Black Friday session
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed up on Friday 27 November, the last completed session, rising 1.6% to 7,297.49 in a shortened post-Thanksgiving session that ended at 1pm New York time. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 591.99 points, or 1.18%, to 50,774.94. The Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.31% to 24,129.50.
Technology shares led the advance. Both the S&P 500 and the Dow finished the week more than 5% higher, according to CNBC, after a sharp sell-off earlier in the month that had pushed the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory, a fall of 10% or more from a peak.
The volatility has been driven by worries over artificial intelligence spending and profits, and by the on-off return of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, which triggered a huge rally on Monday that faded in midweek.
levels.why: Swings in US shares affect pensions, savings and investor confidence worldwide, including in the UK.

levels.headline: US shares rise on Friday, with the S&P 500 up 1.6% to 7,297.49
levels.body:
US stocks closed higher on Friday 27 November, the last full session. The S&P 500 rose 1.6% to 7,297.49. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 591.99 points, or 1.18%, to finish at 50,774.94. The Nasdaq Composite gained 2.31% to close at 24,129.50. Trading ended at 1pm New York time because of the Thanksgiving holiday.
Tech companies led the gains. The S&P 500 and the Dow were both up more than 5% over the week, CNBC reported, recovering from a sell-off that had left them in correction territory, meaning at least 10% below their highs.
Investors remain nervous about how much is being spent on artificial intelligence and whether it will pay off. Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive set off a big rally on Monday, but it faded by Wednesday.
levels.why: US market moves can shift the value of pensions and savings held around the world.

levels.headline: Wall Street rebounds on Friday, with the S&P 500 up 1.6% at 7,297.49
levels.body:
US shares closed higher on Friday 27 November, the last completed session. The S&P 500 gained 1.6% to finish at 7,297.49. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 591.99 points, or 1.18%, to 50,774.94, and the Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.31% to 24,129.50. Markets shut at 1pm New York time because of Thanksgiving.

The swings reflect doubts about whether huge spending on artificial intelligence will pay off, and a rally in Nvidia shares that faded midweek.
levels.why: Moves in US shares can change the value of pensions and savings in the UK and beyond.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends a wild week with a strong rise led by tech shares
levels.body:
Wall Street ended a volatile week on a high. On Friday 27 November, the last completed session, the S&P 500 index closed up 1.6% at 7,297.49. The Dow Jones index rose 1.18% to 50,774.94, a gain of 591.99 points. The tech-heavy Nasdaq rose 2.31% to 24,129.50. Trading stopped at 1pm New York time after Thanksgiving.
The S&P 500 and the Dow both gained more than 5% over the week. That followed a sell-off earlier in the month that pushed them into what traders call a correction, a drop of 10% or more from a peak.
Investors have been unsettled by questions about whether huge spending on artificial intelligence will earn money, and by changes at the top of chipmaker Nvidia.
levels.why: Share prices in the US affect many people's pensions, including in Britain.

levels.headline: US shares go up on Friday after a week of big swings
levels.body:
US shares went up on Friday 27 November, the last day of trading. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big American companies, rose 1.6% to 7,297.49. The Dow Jones, which follows 30 large firms, rose 1.18% to 50,774.94. The Nasdaq, which has many technology firms, rose 2.31% to 24,129.50. The market closed early, at 1pm New York time, after the Thanksgiving holiday.
Tech firms led the rise. Both the S&P 500 and the Dow were up more than 5% on the week, after a sharp fall earlier in November that took them into a correction, which means a drop of 10% or more.
Investors are worried about whether spending on artificial intelligence will pay off.
levels.why: What happens to US shares can affect pensions and savings far away.

levels.headline: American shares rise at the end of a bumpy week
levels.body:
American shares rose on Friday 27 November, the most recent day of trading. The S&P 500, an index of 500 large US companies, rose 1.6% to 7,297.49. The Dow Jones index went up 1.18% to 50,774.94. The Nasdaq, full of technology firms, went up 2.31% to 24,129.50. Shops and markets in the US were quiet because of Thanksgiving, so the stock market shut early at 1pm New York time.
Over the whole week, the S&P 500 and the Dow rose more than 5%. Earlier in the month, they had dropped by 10% or more, which is called a correction.
Many investors are worried about how much money companies are spending on artificial intelligence, or AI.
levels.why: Many pension funds hold US shares, so these moves can matter to ordinary savers.

levels.headline: US share prices went up on Friday

US share prices went up on Friday 27 November. A share is a small piece of a company. People buy and sell them on a stock market. The main measure of the biggest US firms, the S&P 500, rose 1.6% to 7,297.49. The Dow Jones, another measure, rose 1.18% to 50,774.94. The Nasdaq, which has lots of tech firms, rose 2.31% to 24,129.50. The market shut early, at 1pm in New York, for the Thanksgiving holiday.
Over the week, the S&P 500 and the Dow gained more than 5%. Before that, prices had dropped by about a tenth.
Investors worry that firms are spending too much on artificial intelligence, or AI.
levels.why: Lots of people's savings and pensions are tied to share prices.

levels.headline: Shares in America rose on Friday after a shaky few weeks
levels.body:
Shares in America rose on Friday 27 November. Shares are small parts of companies that people can buy. When many shares go up, the stock market is said to rise. The S&P 500, a list of 500 big American companies, went up 1.6% to 7,297.49. The Dow Jones, a list of 30 big companies, went up 1.18% to 50,774.94. The Nasdaq, which has lots of technology firms, went up 2.31% to 24,129.50.
The market closed early at 1pm in New York, because of a holiday called Thanksgiving.
The week was bumpy. Prices fell a lot and then jumped back up. Some people worry that firms are spending too much on artificial intelligence, or AI.
levels.why: Share prices can change how safe people feel about their savings.

levels.headline: American share prices went up on Friday
levels.body:
American share prices went up on Friday. A share is a tiny piece of a company. If lots of people want to buy it, the price goes up. The S&P 500 is a list of 500 big American companies, and its prices went up by 1.6 out of every 100. The Dow, another list, went up by 1.18. The Nasdaq, a list full of tech firms, went up by 2.31. The market closed early because of a holiday called Thanksgiving.
This week prices bounced up and down a lot. They fell, then jumped up, then fell, and then rose again.
Some people are worried that companies are spending too much on artificial intelligence, which is computers that can learn.
levels.why: Share prices tell us how confident people are about big companies.

levels.headline: The American stock market had a happy Friday
levels.body:
Think of the stock market as a big shop where people buy tiny pieces of companies. On Friday, the prices in the shop went up. The list of 500 big American companies, called the S&P 500, went up 1.6%. Two other lists, the Dow and the Nasdaq, went up too. The shop closed early for a holiday called Thanksgiving.
This week was like a seesaw. Prices went down, then up, then down, then up again. At the end of the week, prices were higher than at the start.
Some grown-ups are a little worried. They are not sure if companies that make clever computers will earn enough money.
levels.why: Prices going up and down show how confident grown-ups feel about companies.

headline: Bank of England raises rates to 4% and markets expect another rise on 17 December

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences loan and mortgage costs.
One hundredth of a percentage point.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises rates to 4% and markets expect another rise on 17 December
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised its base rate by 25 basis points, or a quarter of a percentage point, to 4% on 5 November. It was the first increase since 2023. The vote was 8 to 1, with the one dissenting member wanting a 0.5 point rise.
The Bank warned that inflation, which hit 3.5% in September, could approach 5% by the middle of next year. It links this to higher energy prices caused by the conflict involving Iran. Markets still expect more: reports put the chance of another rise at the next decision on 17 December at roughly 75% to 80%, with several further rises priced in by June.
Gilt yields, the interest rates on UK government debt, have been elevated. The ten-year yield has been above 5%. Chancellor John Healey's 28 October Budget was received calmly by investors.
levels.why: Higher rates make mortgages and loans dearer for households and firms, while rewarding savers.

levels.headline: Bank of England lifts rates to 4% and more rises are expected
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised its base rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% on 5 November, its first increase since 2023. Eight of nine members voted for the rise, and the ninth wanted a bigger half-point increase.
The Bank warned that inflation, which reached 3.5% in September, could come close to 5% by the middle of next year. It blames higher energy prices linked to the Iran conflict. Financial markets expect more rises. Reports put the chance of another one on 17 December at around 75% to 80%, with further increases priced in by June.
Yields on gilts, which are UK government bonds, have stayed high, with the ten-year above 5%. Investors reacted calmly to Chancellor John Healey's Budget on 28 October.
levels.why: Higher interest rates make borrowing dearer, which affects mortgages, business loans and savings.

levels.headline: Bank of England lifts rates to 4% for the first time since 2023 and warns on inflation
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised its base rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% on 5 November, its first rise since 2023. Eight members voted for the move and one wanted a half-point rise.
The Bank said inflation, which was 3.5% in September, could come close to 5% by the middle of next year, because of higher energy prices linked to the conflict involving Iran.
Financial markets expect further rises. Reports put the chance of an increase on 17 December at around 75% to 80%. Yields on UK government bonds have stayed high, with the ten-year above 5%.
levels.why: Higher rates make borrowing dearer but reward savers.

levels.headline: The Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%, with more rises expected
levels.body:
The Bank of England put up its main interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point, to 4%, on 5 November. This was its first rise since 2023. Eight members voted for it and one wanted a bigger rise of half a point.
The Bank said inflation, the rate at which prices rise, could get close to 5% by the middle of next year. It was 3.5% in September. The Bank puts this down to higher energy prices linked to the conflict involving Iran. Markets think more rises are coming, with about a 75% to 80% chance of one on 17 December.
The interest rate on government borrowing has also been high, with the ten-year rate above 5%.
levels.why: Higher rates mean dearer loans and mortgages but better returns for savers.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% as it fears prices will keep rising
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates to 4%. It put them up by a quarter of a percentage point on 5 November. This was the first rise since 2023. Eight of its nine decision-makers voted yes. The other wanted a bigger rise.
The Bank is worried about inflation, which is how fast prices go up. It was 3.5% in September. The Bank says it could get close to 5% by the middle of next year because energy costs are higher, linked to the conflict involving Iran.
Markets expect more rises. They think there is about a 75% to 80% chance of another one on 17 December. The Bank's next decision is on that date.
levels.why: Higher interest rates make it dearer to borrow money, such as for a mortgage, and better to save.

levels.headline: The Bank of England puts up interest rates to 4% to try to slow rising prices
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up its interest rate to 4%. The interest rate is the price of borrowing money. The rise was a quarter of a percentage point and it was decided on 5 November. It is the first rise since 2023. Eight of nine members voted for it. One wanted a bigger rise.
The Bank is worried because prices are going up faster. Inflation was 3.5% in September. The Bank thinks it could get close to 5% by the middle of next year, because energy costs more now.
Many investors think the Bank will put rates up again on 17 December. They think this is quite likely, at about three in four or more.
levels.why: A higher rate makes loans and mortgages dearer, but it can help savers and slow price rises.

levels.headline: The Bank of England raises interest rates because prices are going up
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates to 4%. Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow money, or get when you save. The Bank made the rise on 5 November. It was a quarter of a percentage point. It was the first rise since 2023.
The Bank did this because prices are rising faster. That is called inflation. It was 3.5% in September. The Bank thinks it could get close to 5% next year because energy costs more. That is linked to the fighting involving Iran.
Many people who trade money think there will be another rise on 17 December. They think it is quite likely.
levels.why: Higher rates make loans dearer, but they are meant to slow down price rises.

levels.headline: The Bank of England makes borrowing money cost more
levels.body:
The Bank of England is the bank that looks after Britain's money. It has made borrowing money cost more. It did this by raising its interest rate to 4% on 5 November. Interest is the extra you pay back when you borrow money. Eight of the nine people who decide voted for the rise.
They did it because prices are going up too fast. When prices go up, your money buys less. This is called inflation. It was 3.5% in September. The Bank thinks it could reach nearly 5% next year, because energy costs more.
Some people think the Bank will raise the rate again on 17 December.
levels.why: It can make mortgages and loans dearer, but it is trying to keep prices steady.

levels.headline: The Bank that looks after Britain's money has raised its rates
levels.body:
The Bank of England looks after Britain's money. It has a rate of interest, which is the extra money you pay when you borrow. It has raised the rate to 4%. This means that borrowing costs more for families and shops.
The Bank did this because prices keep going up. A packet of crisps that costs 50p now might cost more next year. The Bank wants to slow that down. Prices have been rising because energy costs more, and there is fighting in the Middle East.
Some people think the Bank may raise the rate again on 17 December. We will find out then.
levels.why: It tries to stop prices rising too fast, but borrowing becomes dearer.

levels.headline: The bank for Britain has made borrowing cost more
levels.body:
Imagine you borrow 10 pounds from a friend and you promise to pay back a little extra. That little extra is called interest. The Bank of England is like the big friend that all the other banks borrow from. It has decided that the little extra should be bigger.
The Bank did this because prices are going up. Sweets and bus tickets cost more than before. Making borrowing cost more can slow that down.
It is the first time the Bank has done this since 2023. Grown-ups who pay back loans may have to pay a little more. Grown-ups who save money may get a little more.
levels.why: It is meant to stop prices rising too fast, but it can be hard on people with loans.

headline: EU leaders leave Brussels without a deal on the 2028 to 2034 budget after talks over Ukraine funding collapse

terms.meaning: The seven-year spending plan agreed by all 27 EU countries.
The power to block a decision.

levels.headline: EU leaders leave Brussels without a deal on the 2028 to 2034 budget after talks over Ukraine funding collapse
levels.body:
European Union leaders left Brussels without agreeing the bloc's budget for 2028 to 2034 after a two-day summit ended early on Thursday night. Talks broke down after midnight when German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the fiscally conservative "frugal" countries walked out on European Council President Antonio Costa.
Berlin wants spending cuts and wants Ukraine funding tied to the wider budget. Mr Merz has threatened a veto unless all 27 members sign up. Russian attacks have opened a hole of about 70 billion euros in Ukraine's 2027 budget. The Commission has proposed a 45 billion euro loan, with countries able to opt into a 20 billion euro civilian strand while staying out of a 25 billion euro military strand.
Leaders have set a final deadline for a deal at a summit one week before Christmas.
levels.why: The budget decides what the EU spends for years, and Ukraine's finances depend on the outcome.

levels.headline: EU summit ends early without a budget deal as Ukraine funding splits leaders
levels.body:
European Union leaders went home from Brussels without a deal on the bloc's budget for 2028 to 2034. The two-day summit ended early on Thursday night. After midnight, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and a group of cost-conscious "frugal" countries walked out on European Council President Antonio Costa.
Germany wants spending cuts and wants Ukraine aid tied to the budget, and Mr Merz has threatened to block everything unless all 27 members agree. Russian attacks have left a gap of about 70 billion euros in Ukraine's 2027 budget. The European Commission has offered a 45 billion euro loan, letting countries join the 20 billion euro civilian part and stay out of the 25 billion euro military part.
A final deadline has been set for a summit a week before Christmas.
levels.why: Ukraine's finances and the EU's spending plans for years ahead both hang on the outcome.

levels.headline: EU leaders fail to agree a seven-year budget as a row over Ukraine funding blows up
levels.body:
European Union leaders left Brussels without agreeing the bloc's budget for 2028 to 2034. A two-day summit ended early on Thursday night after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and several cost-conscious countries walked out on European Council President Antonio Costa.
Germany wants spending cuts and wants Ukraine funding tied to the budget. Mr Merz has threatened to block the whole budget unless all 27 members agree. Ukraine faces a gap of about 70 billion euros in its 2027 budget because of Russian attacks, and the Commission has proposed a 45 billion euro loan.
Leaders will try again at a summit a week before Christmas, which has been set as the final deadline.
levels.why: The budget sets EU spending for years, and Ukraine's finances depend on the result.

levels.headline: EU leaders fail to agree a seven-year budget, with Ukraine aid the sticking point
levels.body:
European Union leaders have failed to agree the bloc's budget for 2028 to 2034. Their two-day summit in Brussels finished early on Thursday night. Talks fell apart after midnight when German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the "frugal" countries, which want to limit spending, walked out on European Council President Antonio Costa.
The row is mainly about Ukraine. Germany wants Ukraine funding linked to the wider budget, and Mr Merz has threatened to veto, or block, the budget unless all 27 countries sign up. Russian attacks have left Ukraine about 70 billion euros short for 2027. The Commission suggests a 45 billion euro loan, with countries free to opt out of the 25 billion euro military part.
Leaders now aim to settle it a week before Christmas.
levels.why: The result will affect Ukraine's ability to pay its way and how much EU countries spend.

levels.headline: EU leaders cannot agree on their big spending plan and argue about Ukraine money
levels.body:
Leaders of the European Union could not agree on their spending plan for 2028 to 2034. They met in Brussels for two days, but the summit ended early on Thursday night. After midnight, Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz and several countries that want to spend less walked out on the meeting's chair, Antonio Costa.
The argument is about Ukraine. Germany wants help for Ukraine linked to the main budget. Mr Merz has said he may use a veto, which means blocking the plan, unless all 27 countries agree. Russia's attacks have left a hole of about 70 billion euros in Ukraine's money for 2027. A 45 billion euro loan has been suggested.
The leaders will try again a week before Christmas.
levels.why: Ukraine needs money to keep running, and EU countries need a budget to plan ahead.

levels.headline: European leaders fail to agree a budget, mostly because of money for Ukraine
levels.body:
European leaders have not been able to agree a budget. The European Union is a group of 27 countries. Every few years, they agree a big plan for what to spend. This time the leaders met in Brussels for two days, but the meeting ended early on Thursday night with no deal. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and some countries that want to spend less walked out.
The main argument is about Ukraine, which is being attacked by Russia. Ukraine is short of about 70 billion euros for next year. Germany wants help for Ukraine linked to the budget, and Mr Merz says he could block it all.
They will try again a week before Christmas.
levels.why: If they do not agree, countries cannot plan their spending, and Ukraine could go short.

levels.headline: European leaders could not agree on their big spending plan
levels.body:
European leaders could not agree on a big spending plan. The European Union is a club of 27 countries that work together. They agree a budget, which is a plan for spending money, for several years at a time. This week, the leaders met in Brussels to agree the plan for 2028 to 2034. The meeting ended early on Thursday night with no deal.
The biggest argument is about helping Ukraine, a country at war with Russia. Ukraine is short of about 70 billion euros for next year. Germany's leader, Friedrich Merz, said he might block the plan unless every country agrees to help.
The leaders will meet again a week before Christmas to try once more.
levels.why: The EU's spending plan affects many people, and Ukraine needs help to pay its bills.

levels.headline: European leaders could not agree how to share out money
levels.body:
The leaders of European countries could not agree how to share out money. They belong to the European Union, a group of 27 countries. Every few years they decide how much money to spend and on what. This week they met in a city called Brussels. They talked for two days, but the meeting ended early with no answer.
They are arguing mostly about Ukraine, a country that Russia is attacking. Ukraine is short of lots of money. Some leaders want to give more. Others, like Germany's Friedrich Merz, want to spend less and are saying no for now.
They will meet again just before Christmas and try again.
levels.why: Countries need to agree on money to plan, and Ukraine needs help now.

levels.headline: The leaders of Europe had an argument about money
levels.body:
The leaders of European countries had an argument about money. They went to a big meeting in a city called Brussels. Their job was to agree a plan for how to spend money together over the next seven years. But they could not agree, so the meeting ended early and everyone went home.
Part of the argument was about Ukraine, a country that is in a war and needs help to pay for things. Some leaders wanted to give more. Others wanted to spend less.
They are going to meet again just before Christmas and try to agree. Perhaps they will find a way to be fair to everybody.
levels.why: Countries can only do big things together if they agree on money.

levels.headline: Leaders in Europe could not agree on how to share their money
levels.body:
Imagine the grown-ups of many families all share a big pot of money. They have to decide together how to use it for the next few years. This week they sat down to talk, but they could not agree. Some wanted to spend more and some wanted to spend less. The meeting ended early.
One big question was about a country called Ukraine. It is in a war and needs help with its money. Some of the grown-ups were happy to help. Others were not so sure.
They will try again just before Christmas, and hopefully they will find an answer.
levels.why: Sharing money fairly is hard, but it matters when someone needs help.

headline: UK economy grows 0.7% in the third quarter as AI demand lifts output

terms.meaning: The total value of goods and services an economy produces.
A three-month period of the year.

levels.headline: UK economy grows 0.7% in the third quarter as AI demand lifts output
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, covering July to September, according to the Office for National Statistics, in line with forecasts. Output was 1.9% higher than a year earlier.
Services drove the growth, with information and communication up 2.1%. The ONS said computer programming and consultancy was the largest contributor to GDP growth in 2026, which analysts link to demand for artificial intelligence and cloud computing. CNBC quoted a description of AI as an "extra engine of growth".
The outlook is less bright. Analysts expect growth to slow in the final quarter of 2026 and into 2027. They point to risks from the conflict involving Iran, which has pushed up energy prices, and from higher interest rates after the Bank of England raised its rate to 4%.
levels.why: Growth affects jobs, wages and tax revenues, so a slowdown would make the Chancellor's task harder.

levels.headline: UK economy expands 0.7% in the third quarter, with AI-related services in the lead
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% between July and September, the Office for National Statistics said. That matched forecasts. Compared with a year earlier, output was up 1.9%.
Services led the way. Information and communication rose 2.1%, and the ONS said computer programming and consultancy contributed most to GDP growth this year. Analysts tie that to demand for artificial intelligence and cloud computing.
Economists expect growth to cool in the last three months of 2026 and into 2027. The risks include the conflict involving Iran and its effect on energy prices, and higher borrowing costs after the Bank of England lifted its rate to 4%.
levels.why: Growth drives jobs, pay and tax receipts, so a slowdown would put pressure on households and the Treasury.

levels.headline: UK economy grows 0.7% in the third quarter, with computing and AI services in the lead

The UK economy grew by 0.7% between July and September, the Office for National Statistics reported, matching forecasts. Output was 1.9% higher than a year earlier.

Analysts expect growth to slow in the last quarter of the year and in 2027. The conflict involving Iran has raised energy costs, and the Bank of England has raised interest rates to 4%.
levels.why: Growth affects jobs, pay and tax receipts.

levels.headline: UK economy grows 0.7% in three months as computing and AI services boom
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% from July to September, according to official figures from the Office for National Statistics. This was what experts expected. Compared with a year ago, the economy is 1.9% bigger.
Most of the growth came from services. The area called information and communication grew by 2.1%. The ONS said that computer programming and consultancy did the most to lift growth this year. Analysts say this is because firms want artificial intelligence and cloud computing.
But experts expect things to slow down by the end of the year and in 2027. The conflict involving Iran has raised energy prices, and interest rates have gone up to 4%.
levels.why: A growing economy usually means more jobs and higher pay, so slowing growth matters.

levels.headline: Britain's economy grew by 0.7% between July and September
levels.body:
Britain's economy grew by 0.7% between July and September. This comes from the Office for National Statistics, or ONS, which counts these things. The number is called GDP, the value of everything the country makes and sells. It is 1.9% higher than a year ago.
Most of the growth came from services, such as computing. Companies that write computer programs and give advice were the biggest help. Experts say this is because many firms want artificial intelligence, or AI, and cloud computing.
Experts think growth will slow down soon. Energy costs more because of fighting involving Iran, and interest rates have risen to 4%. That makes borrowing dearer.
levels.why: When the economy grows, there are usually more jobs and higher pay.

levels.headline: Britain's economy grew faster than usual over the summer and autumn
levels.body:
Britain's economy grew by 0.7% between July and September. The Office for National Statistics, which collects official numbers, said so. The measure is called GDP. It shows how much the country makes and sells. It is 1.9% higher than a year ago.
Much of the growth came from services. Computer firms did especially well, as many companies want artificial intelligence, or AI, and storage for their data online.
But experts think growth will slow soon. Energy costs more because of fighting involving Iran. The Bank of England has also raised the interest rate to 4%, which makes borrowing money more expensive for firms.
levels.why: A growing economy can mean more jobs and pay rises, so a slowdown would matter.

levels.headline: Britain's economy grew a little over the last few months
levels.body:
Britain's economy grew by 0.7% between July and September. The people who count these things are called the Office for National Statistics. The number they used is called GDP. It means how much the country makes and sells, like food, computers and haircuts. It is also 1.9% bigger than last year.
A lot of the growth came from companies that work with computers. Many firms want help with artificial intelligence, or AI.
But experts think growth will get slower soon. Energy costs more because of fighting in the Middle East. Borrowing money is also costing more, as interest rates went up to 4%.
levels.why: When the economy grows, there are usually more jobs, but growth may slow.

levels.headline: Britain made and sold more things in the last few months
levels.body:
Britain made and sold more things between July and September. The country's whole total went up by 0.7%. People who count these things said so. The total is called GDP. It means all the things a country makes and sells, like food, cars and computer programs.
A lot of the extra came from computer companies. Many firms want help from AI, which is a computer that can learn to do jobs.
Experts think things may slow down soon. Energy costs more because of fighting far away. Borrowing money costs more too. When firms make and sell less, there can be fewer jobs.
levels.why: When a country does well, more people can find jobs.

levels.headline: Britain did a bit better over the summer
levels.body:
Between July and September, Britain made and sold more than before. Think of a school fair. If you sell more cakes than last time, you did well. The whole country did the same thing, but with all sorts of things, like computer programs and haircuts.
A lot of the extra came from computer companies. Many firms wanted help from AI, which is a clever computer that can learn.
But grown-ups think the good news might not last. Fuel costs more because of fighting far away. Borrowing money costs more, too. If firms sell less, there might not be as many jobs.
levels.why: When a country does well, more families can find work.

levels.headline: Britain sold more cakes and computers than before
levels.body:
Imagine the whole of Britain is one big school fair. Everybody sells things, like cakes, toys and computer games. This summer, Britain sold more at the fair than before. The grown-ups count the money and call it growth.
A lot of the extra came from computer helpers. Some are clever programs called AI that can learn. Many shops want them.
But the grown-ups think the fair might get quieter soon. Fuel costs more, and borrowing costs more too. If fewer people buy things, shops might need fewer helpers. We will see what happens next.
levels.why: When shops do well, more people have work and money.

headline: Brent crude trades near $95 a barrel, heading for a weekly gain as Middle East attacks threaten supply

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil.
The standard unit for oil, about 159 litres.

levels.headline: Brent crude trades near $95 a barrel, heading for a weekly gain as Middle East attacks threaten supply
levels.body:
Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, traded at around $94 to $96 a barrel on Friday 27 November. Trading Economics reported a settlement of $94.95, down 1.49% on the day, while CNBC saw it trading just above $94 at one point, down more than 2%.
Prices were still heading for a weekly gain after Houthi militants, backed by Tehran, struck Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery on the Red Sea, forcing a temporary suspension of some operations. Brent has nonetheless fallen about 15% over the past month.
ANZ analysts say it could rise above $100 even without a major new escalation in the Middle East. The International Energy Agency, by contrast, projects a supply surplus in the fourth quarter.
levels.why: Oil prices feed straight into petrol, heating bills and inflation, and the Bank of England is watching them closely.

levels.headline: Brent crude hovers near $95 as attacks on Gulf energy sites keep prices on edge
levels.body:
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, traded at about $94 to $96 a barrel on Friday 27 November. Trading Economics put the settlement at $94.95, down 1.49% on the day. CNBC reported it trading just above $94 at one point, down more than 2%.
Prices were on course for a weekly rise after Houthi militants, who are backed by Iran, attacked Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery on the Red Sea and forced a temporary halt to some operations. Over the past month, though, Brent has dropped by about 15%.
Analysts at ANZ say it could climb above $100 without any further major escalation. The International Energy Agency expects an oversupply of oil in the fourth quarter.
levels.why: Oil prices affect petrol, home energy bills and inflation, which in turn influences interest rates.

levels.headline: Brent crude hovers near $95 a barrel after Houthi attack on a Saudi refinery
levels.body:
Brent crude, the main international oil price, traded at around $94 to $96 a barrel on Friday 27 November. Trading Economics reported a settlement of $94.95, down 1.49% on the day.
The price was heading for a weekly rise after Houthi militants, who are backed by Iran, attacked Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery on the Red Sea. Some operations were temporarily suspended. Despite that, Brent has fallen about 15% over the last month.
Analysts at ANZ say it could pass $100 a barrel even without a major new escalation, while the International Energy Agency expects a surplus of oil in the fourth quarter.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating and inflation.

levels.headline: Oil prices stay high as attacks in the Middle East threaten supplies
levels.body:
The price of Brent crude, the main international oil benchmark, was around $94 to $96 a barrel on Friday 27 November. Trading Economics said it ended at $94.95, down 1.49%. CNBC said it was just above $94 at one point, down more than 2%.
Still, the price was heading for a rise over the week. Houthi militants backed by Iran hit Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery on the Red Sea, and some operations had to stop for a while. Over the past month, Brent has actually fallen about 15%.
Analysts at ANZ think it could pass $100 even without a big new escalation. The International Energy Agency expects a surplus of oil in the last three months of the year.
levels.why: Oil prices change what people pay for fuel and heating, and can push up prices in shops.

levels.headline: Oil costs about $95 a barrel as attacks in the Middle East worry traders
levels.body:
Oil cost about $94 to $96 a barrel on Friday 27 November. This is the price of Brent crude, the main measure used around the world. A barrel holds about 159 litres. One source said it ended the day at $94.95, down 1.49%.
The price was still on track to rise over the week. Houthi fighters, who are backed by Iran, attacked a big oil refinery in Saudi Arabia called Jazan, on the Red Sea. Some of its work had to stop for a short time. Over the past month, though, the price has fallen about 15%.
Some experts think it could go above $100. Others say there may be too much oil by the end of the year.
levels.why: Higher oil prices can mean dearer petrol, heating and food.

levels.headline: Oil prices stay near $95 a barrel after an attack in the Middle East
levels.body:
Oil prices stayed near $95 a barrel on Friday 27 November. This is the price of Brent crude, which is used as a guide to oil prices around the world. A barrel is a big container of oil.
The price went up over the week because of an attack. Houthi fighters, who are supported by Iran, hit a big oil plant in Saudi Arabia. The plant is called the Jazan refinery. Some of its work stopped for a while. Even so, the price is about 15% lower than it was a month ago.
Some experts think the price could go above $100. Others think there will soon be more oil than the world needs.
levels.why: Oil is used for petrol and heating, so its price touches almost everyone.

levels.headline: The price of oil is about $95 a barrel after an attack on a refinery
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid that comes from under the ground. It is used to make petrol and many other things. On Friday, a barrel of oil cost about $95. A barrel is a big container.
The price went up this week because of an attack. A group called the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, hit a refinery in Saudi Arabia. A refinery is a factory that turns oil into things we can use. Some work there had to stop for a while. Even so, the price is lower than it was a month ago.
Some experts think the price could pass $100. Others think there will be plenty of oil soon.
levels.why: When oil costs more, petrol and heating can cost more too.

levels.headline: The price of oil is high after an attack in the Middle East
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid from under the ground. We use it to make petrol for cars. On Friday, a big container of oil cost about $95. That is a lot of money.
The price went up this week because of an attack. A group of fighters attacked a factory in Saudi Arabia, which is far away from the UK. The factory turns oil into petrol and other things. Some of its work had to stop for a while. That makes people worry there will not be enough oil.
When people worry, the price goes up. Some experts think it could go even higher. Others think there will be enough oil soon.
levels.why: When oil gets dearer, petrol and heating can cost more for families.

levels.headline: Oil costs a lot because of trouble far away
levels.body:
Oil is a thick, dark liquid that comes from under the ground. Cars use it to make petrol, and some homes use it to stay warm. This week, a big container of oil cost about $95, which is a lot.
There was trouble far away, in Saudi Arabia. Some fighters attacked a factory that turns oil into petrol. Some of the work there had to stop for a while. When people think there might not be enough of something, they will pay more for it.
Some experts think oil will cost even more soon. Others think there will be plenty of it.
levels.why: When oil costs more, petrol and heating can cost more for families.

levels.headline: Oil costs more when people worry there will not be enough
levels.body:
Imagine you are selling lemonade at a fair. If the lemons run low, you might charge more for each cup. That is how the price of oil works too.
Oil is a thick, dark liquid from under the ground. We use it to make petrol for cars. This week, some fighters attacked an oil factory in a country far away, and some of its work had to stop. People worried there might not be enough oil. So the price went up a bit.
At the same time, the price is lower than it was a month ago. When oil is dear, the things we buy can cost more.
levels.why: Oil is used in so many things that its price can change what we pay.

headline: Estonia to close all five road crossings with Russia on 1 December for six months

terms.meaning: Russia's military intelligence agency.
Penalties, such as trade limits, imposed on a country.

levels.headline: Estonia to close all five road crossings with Russia on 1 December for six months
levels.body:
Estonia will close all five of its road border crossings with Russia at 7am on 1 December for an initial six months. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna confirmed the plan on 27 November during a visit to Baku. The crossings are Narva-1, Narva-2, Koidula, Luhamaa and Saatse. Rail freight through Narva will continue, subject to sanctions.
Tallinn blames Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, for an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems near Tallinn on 14 November. Eight Latvian citizens were detained and are suspected of being recruited for the operation. Estonia says closing the border will make recruitment and sanctions evasion harder.
Moscow denies involvement and has accused Estonia of hostile actions that put it "on the verge of unleashing open war". Estonia rejects that. Travellers will have to go via Latvia.
levels.why: It is a sharp escalation between a NATO member and Russia, and it will disrupt families and travellers.

levels.headline: Estonia confirms it will shut its road border with Russia from 1 December
levels.body:
Estonia will close all five road crossings with Russia at 7am on 1 December, initially for six months. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna confirmed this on 27 November while visiting Baku. The crossings are Narva-1, Narva-2, Koidula, Luhamaa and Saatse. Rail freight through Narva will carry on under sanctions rules.
Estonia says Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, was behind an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems near Tallinn on 14 November. Eight Latvians were detained, and investigators think they were recruited for the job. The government says closing the border will make such recruitment, and sanctions evasion, harder.
Russia denies any role and says Estonia's actions bring it "on the verge of unleashing open war". Estonia rejects that claim.
levels.why: A NATO country is cutting links with Russia, which raises tension and affects many families.

levels.headline: Estonia will close its five road border crossings with Russia from 1 December
levels.body:
Estonia will close all five of its road crossings with Russia at 7am on 1 December, at first for six months. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna confirmed this on 27 November. Freight trains through Narva will still run under sanctions rules.
The government blames Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, for an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems near Tallinn on 14 November. Eight Latvian citizens were detained. Estonia says the closure will make it harder for Russia to recruit people and to avoid sanctions.
Russia denies any part in the attack and says Estonia is acting in a hostile way. Estonia rejects this. Travellers will need to go through Latvia.
levels.why: It raises tension between Russia and a NATO member and will disrupt families and travellers.

levels.headline: Estonia to close its road border with Russia for six months
levels.body:
Estonia will shut all five of its road crossings with Russia from 7am on 1 December, at first for six months. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna confirmed the move on 27 November. Trains carrying freight through Narva will still run, as long as they follow sanctions rules.
The government says Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, tried to set fire to the premises of drone maker Threod Systems near Tallinn on 14 November. Eight Latvian citizens were arrested. Moscow denies it was involved and says Estonia is acting in a hostile way. Estonia rejects this.
levels.why: The move raises tension between NATO and Russia, and it changes daily life for people who cross the border.

levels.headline: Estonia will close its road crossings with Russia for six months
levels.body:
Estonia will close all five road crossings into Russia at 7am on 1 December. The closure is planned for six months. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said so on 27 November. Freight trains through the town of Narva will still be allowed, as long as they follow sanctions, which are rules that limit trade with Russia.
The government says Russia's military spy agency, the GRU, tried to burn down the building of a drone maker near the capital, Tallinn, on 14 November. Eight people from Latvia were arrested. Estonia thinks closing the border will make it harder for spies to find helpers.
Russia says it had nothing to do with it. It says Estonia is acting in a hostile way.
levels.why: It increases tension between Russia and a NATO country, and it will affect families and travellers.

levels.headline: Estonia is going to close its roads to Russia for six months
levels.body:
Estonia is going to close all five of its road crossings to Russia. The closing time is 7am on 1 December, and it will last for six months at first. Estonia's foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, said this on 27 November. Trains carrying goods will still run.
The government says Russian spies tried to set fire to a building owned by a firm that makes drones, near the capital, Tallinn. This was on 14 November. Eight people from Latvia, a nearby country, were held by the police. Estonia thinks the spies hired people who came across the border.
Russia says it had nothing to do with the fire. It says Estonia is being hostile. Estonia says that is not true.
levels.why: It makes a tense situation between Russia and its neighbours worse.

levels.headline: Estonia will shut its road border with Russia for six months
levels.body:
Estonia is a small country next to Russia. It has decided to close all five of its road border crossings to Russia. The border will close at 7am on 1 December and stay shut for six months. Cars and lorries will not be able to cross. Trains with goods can still go through.
The reason is a fire attack on 14 November. Estonia says Russian spies tried to burn down a building owned by a company that makes drones. Eight people from Latvia were arrested. Estonia thinks the spies pay people to do jobs like this.
Russia says it did nothing wrong and is angry with Estonia. People who need to cross will have to go a longer way round.
levels.why: It shows how worried countries near Russia are about spying and attacks.

levels.headline: A small country in Europe is closing its roads to Russia
levels.body:
Estonia is a small country in Europe. It has a border with Russia, which is a very big country. There are five roads across the border where cars and lorries cross. From 1 December, Estonia will close all five for six months.
The leaders of Estonia say Russian spies tried to start a fire at a factory that makes drones. Drones are flying machines with no pilot. They say closing the border will make it harder for spies to come and go. Russia says it did not do it, and it is angry about the closing.
Some families live on both sides of the border. They will find it much harder to visit each other.
levels.why: The decision shows how tense things are, and it will make life harder for some families.

levels.headline: A country called Estonia will close its roads to Russia
levels.body:
Estonia is a small country, and Russia is a very big country next door. There are five roads where people can drive from one to the other. Estonia has decided to close all five roads for six months, starting on 1 December.
The leaders of Estonia say that spies from Russia tried to start a fire at a place that makes drones. Drones are little flying machines. Estonia wants to stop spies from sneaking in. Russia says it did not do it and is cross with Estonia.
Some families have people living on both sides. It will be harder for them to see each other.
levels.why: It shows that countries try to protect themselves when they feel unsafe.

levels.headline: A little country shuts its gates to a big neighbour
levels.body:
Imagine two houses next to each other. One house is small and the other is very big. The small house has five gates into the big house's garden. Now the small house says it will lock all five gates for a while.
That is what Estonia, a small country, is doing with Russia, its big neighbour. Estonia thinks that people from Russia have been sneaking in to cause trouble, including a fire at a factory. Russia says it did nothing wrong.
Locking the gates will make people feel safer in Estonia. But it also means that families who live on both sides cannot visit each other so easily.
levels.why: People close gates when they feel unsafe, but closing them can hurt families.

headline: One in four UK firms expect turnover to fall in December, ONS survey finds

terms.meaning: The total money a business takes in from sales.
The Office for National Statistics, the UK's official data body.

levels.headline: One in four UK firms expect turnover to fall in December, ONS survey finds
levels.body:
A survey from the Office for National Statistics, published on 19 November, found that 25% of trading businesses expect their turnover to fall in December. Turnover is the total money a business takes in from sales.
Energy prices were the most common factor behind rising prices at firms, cited by 33% of businesses. That fits with the wider picture of higher energy costs linked to the conflict involving Iran, which the Bank of England says could push inflation towards 5% by the middle of next year.
The findings come after GDP grew 0.7% in the third quarter, a result that analysts expect to be followed by a slowdown in the final quarter of 2026. The Bank has also raised interest rates to 4%, increasing borrowing costs for firms.
levels.why: It gives an early sign of how businesses are coping with high energy costs and dearer borrowing going into Christmas.

levels.headline: A quarter of UK businesses expect lower turnover in December, says ONS
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics reported on 19 November that 25% of trading businesses expect their turnover to fall in December. Turnover means the money a business takes from selling its goods or services.
When firms were asked what was pushing up their prices, 33% named energy costs, the most common answer. This matches a wider rise in energy prices linked to the conflict involving Iran. The Bank of England warns that inflation could approach 5% by the middle of next year.
The survey follows 0.7% GDP growth in the third quarter, which analysts expect to slow in the final three months of 2026. The Bank has also raised interest rates to 4%, making loans more expensive for businesses.
levels.why: It shows how firms are feeling about the Christmas period and rising costs.

levels.headline: A quarter of UK trading businesses expect lower turnover in December, the ONS says

A survey from the Office for National Statistics, published on 19 November, found that 25% of trading businesses expect their turnover to fall in December. Turnover is the money a business takes in from sales.
Businesses also said what was pushing up their prices. Energy costs were the most common answer, given by 33% of firms. Energy has become dearer because of the conflict involving Iran.
The survey follows 0.7% GDP growth in the third quarter, which analysts think will slow. The Bank of England has also raised interest rates to 4%, which makes borrowing more expensive for firms.
levels.why: It shows how firms feel about trading over Christmas.

levels.headline: One in four UK businesses think their sales will drop in December
levels.body:
A survey by the Office for National Statistics, published on 19 November, found that one in four trading businesses, 25%, expect their turnover to fall in December. Turnover is the amount of money a business takes in from sales.
The survey also asked what was making prices rise. Energy costs were named most often, by 33% of firms. Energy has become dearer because of the conflict involving Iran, and the Bank of England says inflation could get close to 5% by the middle of next year.
This comes after the economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter. Experts expect growth to slow. Interest rates have also risen to 4%, so borrowing costs more.
levels.why: It suggests many firms are worried about trading over the Christmas period.

levels.headline: A quarter of UK businesses expect to sell less in December
levels.body:
A survey by the Office for National Statistics, or ONS, found that 25% of UK businesses that are trading expect to sell less in December. That is one in four. The survey was published on 19 November. Turnover means the money a business takes in from sales.
Businesses were also asked why their prices were going up. The most common answer was energy costs, which 33% of firms mentioned. Energy has become dearer because of the fighting involving Iran.
The survey comes after the economy grew 0.7% over the summer. But experts think growth will slow. Interest rates have risen to 4%, so it costs more for firms to borrow.
levels.why: December is a key month for shops, so worries about sales matter.

levels.headline: One in four businesses in the UK think they will sell less in December
levels.body:
One in four businesses in the UK think they will sell less in December. That is what a survey by the Office for National Statistics found. The survey came out on 19 November. The exact number was 25% of firms that are trading. Turnover is the money a firm gets from selling things.
The survey also asked why prices were rising. About a third of firms, 33%, said energy costs. Energy costs more because of fighting involving Iran.
The economy grew over the summer, but experts think it may slow. The Bank of England has also raised interest rates to 4%. That means loans cost more, which can be hard for businesses.
levels.why: December is a big month for shops, and worried firms may hire or spend less.

levels.headline: Many UK shops and firms think they will sell less in December
levels.body:
Many UK firms think they will sell less in December. A group called the Office for National Statistics asked businesses what they expect. It found that one in four firms, 25%, think the money they take in will go down. The survey came out on 19 November.
The survey also asked why prices are going up. About a third of firms said it was because energy costs more. Energy is dearer because of fighting involving Iran.
December is usually a busy time for shops, because of Christmas. If people spend less, firms may earn less. Interest rates are higher too, so it costs more for firms to borrow.
levels.why: If firms sell less, it can affect jobs and prices.

levels.headline: One in four businesses think they will sell less in December
levels.body:
A group of people who count things in Britain asked firms a question. They asked how much they think they will sell in December. One in four firms said they think they will sell less. The answer came out on 19 November.
They also asked why prices are going up. Many firms said it is because energy costs more. Energy is what we use for heat and light. It costs more because of fighting far away.
December is a busy month, because of Christmas. If firms sell less, they may have less money to pay workers. Borrowing money costs more too, which is hard for firms.
levels.why: If firms sell less, there may be fewer jobs and less pay.

levels.headline: Some shops think there will be fewer shoppers in December
levels.body:
Some shops and firms think there will be fewer shoppers in December. A group of people who count things in Britain asked them. One in four said they think they will sell less. This is when lots of people usually buy presents.
They also asked why prices are going up. Many said it is because energy, which gives us heat and light, costs more. That is because of fighting far away.
When shops sell less, they have less money to pay their workers. Grown-ups are watching to see what happens.
levels.why: When shops do badly, fewer jobs may be available.

levels.headline: Some shops are worried that fewer people will buy presents
levels.body:
Imagine you run a little shop before Christmas. You hope lots of people will come and buy things. But some of the shopkeepers in Britain are worried. One in four of them said they think they will sell less this December.
They are worried because it costs more to keep the lights and heating on. It costs more to borrow money, too. When it costs more to run a shop, the shopkeeper may need to charge more.
If you charge more, people might buy less. That is the worry that some shopkeepers have right now.
levels.why: When shops do badly, workers and families can feel it.

headline: Iran denies responsibility after two Italians are killed in a drone attack in Kuwait

terms.meaning: An unmanned aircraft, often used to carry out attacks.

levels.headline: Iran denies responsibility after two Italians are killed in a drone attack in Kuwait
levels.body:
Two Italian specialists working for the arms company Rheinmetall were killed in Kuwait during an attack on the country's military facilities, and Iran has denied any responsibility. Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told the Senate that several Iranian drones hit sites at around 2pm local time, including an air defence radar centre where the two men were working.
Kuwait's army said the Italians died from falling missile debris after it intercepted "a number of hostile" Iranian drones, and four people were injured. Kuwait's Emir called it "a heinous Iranian aggression". Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, called the accusations baseless, proposed a joint investigation with Rome and Kuwait City, and expressed regret. Iran's military accused the US and Israel of staging a false flag attack.
Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar and the UAE condemned the attack. President Donald Trump said the Iran war ends "whenever I want it".
levels.why: It widens a war that already threatens energy supplies, and it now involves a European country's citizens.

headline: Spain goes to the polls on Sunday in a snap election dominated by housing and Pedro Sánchez

terms.meaning: An election called earlier than planned.
A government made up of more than one party.

levels.headline: Spain goes to the polls on Sunday in a snap election dominated by housing and Pedro Sánchez
levels.body:
Spain holds a general election on Sunday 29 November after Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap vote. He did so after parliament rejected measures meant to ease public anger over the country's housing crisis, which had triggered mass protests.
Polls suggest his Socialist-led coalition could lose power. Most predict a win for the right-wing Popular Party, which would then govern in coalition with the far-right party Vox. Housing, inflation and immigration are the key issues, and Mr Sánchez's relationship with US President Donald Trump has been a talking point.
Spain has been governing without a new national budget since 2023, using the 2022 budget. Mr Sánchez skipped this week's EU budget summit in Brussels because of the election, handing his vote to French President Emmanuel Macron.
levels.why: A change of government in Spain, a major EU economy, could shift Europe's politics and policies on housing and migration.

levels.why: Spain is one of Europe's biggest economies, so who wins matters across the EU.

levels.body:

levels.why: Spain's choice affects housing policy and its role in Europe.

The things people care about most are housing, prices and immigration, which is people moving to live in a new country.
levels.why: Housing costs worry people in many countries, and Spain's vote shows how much.

Many people think he might lose. They think a party called the Popular Party might win. It is on the right of politics. It might need help from another party called Vox.
People say the big worries are the cost of homes, the cost of food and bills, and people moving into Spain from other countries.
levels.why: The result decides what Spain does about housing and money.

levels.headline: Spain is having an election to choose a leader
levels.body:

Some people think he will lose. They think another party might win. Different parties want to do different things about homes, prices and people who move to Spain from other places.
In an election, every grown-up gets to say what they think by voting. The party with the most support gets to run the country.
levels.why: Elections let people choose who makes the big decisions.

levels.why: Voting lets people choose who will help with problems like homes.

levels.headline: A country called Spain will choose who is in charge

On Sunday, a country called Spain will do something like that, but for the whole country. It is called an election. Grown-ups will choose who is in charge.
The grown-ups are upset about one thing in particular. Homes cost so much money that some families cannot find a place to live. They will choose the leader they think will help the most.
levels.why: Voting lets everyone have a say about who is in charge.

headline: Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang sparks a huge rally that fades within two days

terms.meaning: A company that designs or makes computer chips.
Initial public offering: when a company first sells shares to the public.

levels.headline: Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang sparks a huge rally that fades within two days
levels.body:
Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday 23 November, eleven days after he resigned on 12 November. Nvidia shares jumped about 31% that day. The S&P 500 rose 4.7% and the Nasdaq Composite 6.5%, both their best days since April 2025. President Donald Trump said he had pressed the board directly to bring Mr Huang back.
The rally faded quickly. Nvidia fell about 5.9% on Tuesday and a further 4% on Wednesday, and Anthropic's shares dropped below their $83 IPO price. A hot inflation reading added worries that higher rates could hurt growth stocks.
Investors remain concerned about artificial intelligence spending and profits, data centre approvals and chip exports to China. Some strategists think the market has bottomed, while others call the bounce a counter-trend rally. Stocks then rebounded on Friday.
levels.why: Nvidia is a bellwether for the AI boom, so its swings move whole markets and pension funds.

levels.headline: A big computer company's boss is back, and share prices bounced up and down
levels.body:
There is a big company called Nvidia. It makes the parts that help computers think. Its boss, Jensen Huang, had left his job. Then, on 23 November, he came back. When he came back, the price of shares in the company jumped up. A share is a tiny piece of a company.
But the happy mood did not last long. After two days, the price went down again. Some people are worried that firms are spending lots of money on computers that can learn, called AI, and may not get the money back.
So prices have been going up and down like a seesaw.
levels.why: When big companies go up and down, other prices move with them.

levels.headline: A big company's boss came back, and prices went up and down
levels.body:
There is a very big company that makes the brains inside smart computers. Its boss left, and then he came back. When he came back, lots of people were happy. They bought pieces of the company, called shares, and the price shot up.
But a few days later, people felt worried again. Some thought the company might not make as much money as hoped. So many people sold their pieces and the price came back down.
It is like a seesaw. Everyone is waiting to see if the clever computers will really earn lots of money.
levels.why: Prices go up and down when people feel happy or worried.

levels.headline: A seesaw of happy and worried feelings about computers
levels.body:
Imagine a toy shop that sells a very special toy. Everyone wants one. One day, the shop's boss, who had gone away, comes back. Everyone is so happy that they rush to buy toys, and the toys cost more.
But a few days later, people start to wonder, "Do we really need so many?" Some people feel worried and stop buying. The price goes back down.
That is a bit like what happened with a big company that makes parts for clever computers. Its shares went up and then down, like a seesaw, because people's feelings kept changing.
levels.why: Feelings of happiness and worry can change prices.
